opus-5.5.text:
I think of it less as AI replacing scientists and more as changing where human judgment sits in the loop. In a traditional lab, a huge fraction of a scientist's time goes into execution: setting up experiments, running assays, cleaning data, troubleshooting protocols. An autonomous lab can take on a lot of that, running many iterations in parallel, around the clock, and learning from each round.

That frees people to focus on the parts that are hardest to automate: deciding which questions actually matter, framing hypotheses in a way that's meaningful, and noticing when a result is surprising in an interesting way versus just noisy. I picture the scientist as something like a principal investigator for a very capable, very fast team. You set direction, you review what comes back, you push on the reasoning, and you make the calls about what's worth pursuing next.

I also think the interaction has to be genuinely collaborative and transparent. The system should be able to explain why it chose a particular experiment, what it expected to see, and how confident it is in its conclusions. Scientists need to be able to interrogate that, disagree with it, and redirect it. Trust in science comes from being able to check the work, and that doesn't change just because an AI is doing more of it.

And there's an important safety and responsibility dimension. Especially in areas like biology, you want humans setting the boundaries: what kinds of experiments are in scope, what requires additional review, where the guardrails are. Autonomy in execution doesn't mean autonomy in deciding what's appropriate to do.

So my hope is that it makes science more ambitious. If the cost of trying an idea drops dramatically, scientists can explore more boldly and test things that would have been too slow or expensive before. The human role becomes more about taste, curiosity, and responsibility, which, honestly, are the parts of science most people got into it for in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says scientists set direction by choosing important questions and framing hypotheses.

r002.rationale: It describes scientists reviewing what the lab returns and deciding what is worth pursuing next.

r003.rationale: It describes scientist–AI feedback and redirection, but does not compare that interaction to working with Codex.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is less as a replacement and more as a shift in what the human's job actually is.

Right now a scientist spends an enormous fraction of their time on execution. Setting up the experiment, debugging the pipeline, waiting for results, rerunning because something was misconfigured. In an autonomous lab, most of that goes away. The AI can propose hypotheses, design the experiments, run them, and iterate on its own, often overnight, across many parallel threads. So what's left for the human is the part that was always the most valuable anyway: deciding what questions are worth asking, and judging whether an answer is actually meaningful.

Concretely, I imagine the interaction looking something like a research group meeting, except the group never sleeps. The scientist comes in and the lab has a set of results waiting, along with the reasoning behind why it ran those experiments. The human reads that, pushes back, says "this direction looks promising but I don't trust the control here," or "you're optimizing a metric that doesn't capture what we care about," and redirects. Taste and skepticism become the main inputs.

I also think the human role in setting boundaries matters a lot. An autonomous system will happily explore whatever space you give it, so someone has to define what's in scope, what's safe, what resources it can use, and when it should stop and ask. Those constraints are scientific decisions as much as safety ones.

And honestly, the thing I'm most excited about is that it lowers the barrier. You don't need a huge lab or years of infrastructure experience to test an idea. If you have a good question, you can get a real answer in days instead of a year. That changes who gets to do science, not just how fast it goes.

r001.rationale: It says the human scientist decides which questions are worth asking and redirects the lab toward promising directions.

r002.rationale: It describes the lab presenting results and its reasoning to the scientist, who critiques them and redirects what the lab investigates.

r003.rationale: The response compares the interaction to a research group meeting, but does not compare it to iterative task-and-feedback interaction with Codex.

astra-6.text:
I imagine it being a very collaborative relationship. Human scientists would help define the questions worth pursuing: What do we want to understand? Why does it matter? What would count as a meaningful result? And an autonomous AI lab could take on more of the work of turning those questions into experiments, running them, analyzing the results, and proposing what to try next.

But I wouldn’t want that to be a black box where you submit a question and get a paper back. Scientists should be able to see the evidence, challenge an assumption, or redirect an experiment. And the AI should be able to come back and say, “This result doesn’t fit our hypothesis. Here are a few possible explanations. What do you think?”

The exciting possibility is that scientists could spend less time on repetitive execution and more time thinking deeply about what the results mean—and asking questions they wouldn’t have had the resources to explore before.

r001.rationale: It says human scientists would define which questions are worth pursuing and what would count as a meaningful result.

r002.rationale: It describes the AI reporting a result that conflicts with the hypothesis, offering possible explanations, and asking scientists what they think; it also says the AI can propose what to try next.

r003.rationale: The response describes collaboration and feedback but does not compare it to iterative task-and-feedback interaction with Codex.

sol-6.1.text:
I imagine it being a very collaborative relationship. Human scientists would help define which questions matter, what success looks like, and what constraints the research should respect. The AI lab could then explore ideas, run experiments, analyze results, and bring back evidence for people to evaluate.

But I wouldn’t want that interaction to be just, “Give it a goal and come back for the answer.” Scientists should be able to inspect the reasoning, challenge assumptions, and redirect the work along the way. And the lab should surface uncertainty—where the evidence is weak, where an experiment failed, or where it needs human judgment.

Ideally, that gives scientists more room to do the creative work: asking better questions, connecting ideas, and deciding what’s worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: It says human scientists define which questions matter and what success looks like, establishing their role in setting high-level research direction.

r002.rationale: It says the AI lab brings back evidence for people to evaluate and that scientists can redirect the work, including deciding what is worth pursuing next.

r003.rationale: It does not compare interaction with the AI lab to iterative task-and-feedback interaction with Codex.
